summary: Weekly POC sync focused on follow-up from yesterday's reliability incident. Discussed observed 5xxs and timeouts, traffic patterns, rate-limiting behavior and retries. transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-19 10:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sara Lopez (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Redwood CSM); Priya Sharma (Nexa Head of ML), Marc Diaz (Nexa Platform Eng), Aisha Khan (Nexa SRE), Ben Russell (Nexa Product)

[00:00] Sara Lopez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to follow up on the incident yesterday and run through the POC status. Quick intro, then Daniel will walk through the logs and proposed mitigations.
[00:18] Priya Sharma: Thanks, Sara. Yep, high level - yesterday from 14:05 to about 14:28 UTC we saw an elevated 5xx rate from the hosted endpoints that drove user visible errors. Aisha's team filed the pager. We reopened the replay and saw timeouts on longer context requests.
[00:32] Daniel Kim: Right, thanks Priya. I pulled preliminary logs from our routing layer and runtime. To be clear, transcription and names might be a little off in this export. But the core thing we saw is a spike in queue time and then a subset of requests hit our upstream model worker that returned 5xx internal errors, followed by increased retries from the client.
[00:54] Marc Diaz: Can you define "queue time" for us? Is that at the rex-serve layer or at the GPU worker queue?
[01:03] Daniel Kim: Good question - queue time here refers to our request queue inside the serving runtime, so before the request is dispatched to a worker. When the runtime is overloaded for a short burst it accumulates requests and we hit the request timeout window which surfaced as client timeouts or our internal 5xxs when the worker aborted.
[01:20] Aisha Khan: From our side we saw a pattern where medium-length prompts (2-3k tokens) had higher failure rates. Short prompts (~<256 tokens) were fine. Also we had some traffic pattern change when our front-end started a batch of concurrent background evaluations around 14:00.
[01:36] Daniel Kim: That matches what we see - a bump in concurrent open streams. We also noted that some requests entered the retry loop quickly because the client library default backoff was minimal. The retries compounded the load.
[01:50] Priya Sharma: Our questions: could this be fixed by tuning client retry/backoff? Or do we need dedicated capacity? We're sensitive to cost but we need reliability.
[02:01] Sara Lopez: Short answer - both. There are mitigations you can apply immediately on client side, and then there are infra-level options like dedicated pools and route-level SLOs. Daniel, can you list the tuning suggestions?
[02:10] Daniel Kim: Sure. Immediate recommendations: increase client-side request timeout for long context requests to 90s, set exponential backoff starting at 500ms with jitter and cap retries to 3, and limit concurrency per client to avoid head-of-line bursts. On the server side we recommend enabling prefix KV cache for repeated prefixes, and increasing worker queue depth for the route.
[02:32] Marc Diaz: The prefix KV cache - is that something we can toggle from our config or do you need to enable it on your side?
[02:39] Daniel Kim: If you're on Hosted, we can enable tuned caching policies for your tenant; for Dedicated you'd control it via config. There's a small latency cost for cache warmups but for repeated prompt patterns it's net win. Sorry if I said Redwood Dedicate earlier in a call - auto transcription sometimes munges names.
[02:57] Ben Russell: No worries. Regarding rate limits, we got a 429 in a few traces right before the 5xxs. Is that part of the same cascade?
[03:06] Daniel Kim: Yep, likely. Rate limiters kicked in for a subset of front-end nodes as the queue grew. Some of the 429s were followed by immediate retries from the client, which then hit the queue and pushed more requests into workers - classic retry storm.
[03:24] Aisha Khan: We can add client-side backoff quickly. We also wanted to confirm retention of logs - we saw partial logs in the console but need full request IDs for our tracing. Can Redwood export those?
[03:36] Ravi Patel: We can export an incident bundle with the request IDs, routing traces, and worker logs. I'll own that deliverable. We'll redact sensitive fields but include timestamps and correlation IDs.
[03:47] Priya Sharma: Great. For compliance we'll need to know if any customer data was persisted in traces or long-term logs.
[03:56] Daniel Kim: We don't persist full request payloads by default in long-term logs; the incident bundle includes traces and short metadata. If you need a fully sanitized trace set we can provide a redacted bundle and sign a NDA for deeper logs.
[04:12] Marc Diaz: On retries - can the platform do smarter retry suppression? We were thinking of server-side retry-coalescing or sticky routing to avoid sending the same retried request to a cold worker.
[04:23] Daniel Kim: We have some mechanisms - sticky worker allocations and request dedupe for idempotent calls are in our roadmap. For today, we can apply route-level rate limits and adaptive queue thresholds. That will reduce head-of-line blocking.
[04:38] Priya Sharma: Timeline question - if we accept Redwood's config suggestions and do client changes, how soon can we validate in staging?
[04:46] Sara Lopez: We can get a staging config pushed within 48 hours once we get the failing request IDs and sample payloads. Then you can run a replay; Daniel's team will be available to watch the replay.
[04:56] Aisha Khan: We'll try to replay the load on Tuesday and share the results.
[05:01] Daniel Kim: Also, for longer-term reliability if you need hard SLOs during peak hours we can discuss a Dedicated pool with reserved GPUs, which reduces queue variability. There is a delta in cost but predictable latency.
[05:14] Ben Russell: Do you have a quick ballpark for monthly cost for a minimal dedicated pool for our load? We currently peak ~20 rps of medium context and 5 rps of long context during eval windows.
[05:26] Sara Lopez: We can send a tailored estimate after we profile the replay. I'll include committed commit tiers and burst options in the deck I send.
[05:34] Marc Diaz: One more technical note - we noticed A/B tests where some routes used function-calling which increased token churn. Could that have exacerbated the worker load?
[05:46] Daniel Kim: Function-calling can increase token generation steps if you have long tool outputs. It can also change batching characteristics. For the incident, we saw a cluster of requests with tool calls - so yes it's probably a factor.
[05:58] Priya Sharma: Ok, sounds like action plan is: Redwood provides logs + suggested config, Nexa runs replay with client-side backoff changes, and we schedule deep-dive if issues persist. Anything else?
[06:12] Ravi Patel: I'll also propose tuned retry/backoff sample code snippets for your SDKs and a sample helm values file if you're self-hosting or using Dedicated.
[06:24] Aisha Khan: Please include guidance on safe timeout limits for streaming vs non-streaming calls.
[06:30] Daniel Kim: Will do. We'll recommend 90s for long non-streaming, and keep streaming timeouts higher with heartbeat pings. Also we'll suggest server-side health checks to drop stuck worker sessions earlier.
[06:46] Ben Russell: Any security or compliance asks from this incident?
[06:50] Sara Lopez: Nothing new - we'll share the redacted incident bundle and the security docs link (https://redwood.example.com/security.pdf). If you want an SOC2 or ISO attest, our sales team can route that.
[07:05] Priya Sharma: Great. Could you also note any code changes that might be needed for our client? We use a wrapped SDK in node and a python job for replays.
[07:16] Daniel Kim: We'll produce examples for both node and python showing the backoff, retry caps, and concurrency limiter. Also we'll include a suggestion to send an idempotency key for requests so the platform can dedupe if needed.
[07:30] Sara Lopez: Ok let's recap next steps. Daniel, logs and proposed config by Friday. Aisha and Priya will run a replay on Tuesday and send results. Ravi will schedule a deep-dive if replay shows residual errors. I'll send pricing/commit options.
[07:49] Priya Sharma: Thanks all. Quick timeline call-out - our procurement is on a tight cadence; if we need Dedicated we may want to move fast.
[07:58] Sara Lopez: Understood, we'll prioritize the follow-ups.
[08:03] Marc Diaz: Minor transcription glitch - the export says "KV cache" as "KV cash" in a line but we understood.
[08:10] (laughter)
[08:15] Sara Lopez: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the attachments.
[08:20] Meeting ended.

Notes: Transcript has occasional mis-attributions and minor transcription errors consistent with automated meeting exports. References to docs and links: incident bundle placeholder, security doc link above, pricing deck (to be shared).
